# HyperFund / HyperVerse: Investigation of the Alleged Crypto Fraud Network

## Executive assessment

The available evidence supports a strong, evidence-based assessment that HyperFund—later rebranded as HyperVerse and HyperNation—was structured around a combination of alleged Ponzi and pyramid-scheme mechanics. Its recruitment system promised unusually high passive returns, represented that those returns were funded by large-scale cryptocurrency mining, and rewarded members for recruiting others. When withdrawals became difficult, the operation appears to have relied on rebranding and new narratives rather than demonstrating a legitimate revenue source. The launch of HyperVerse also featured a purported chief executive, “Steven Reece Lewis,” whose identity and résumé were questioned by investigative reporting and later described by the SEC as fabricated and performed by a paid actor. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases); [S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11); [S3](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist))

This conclusion remains legally qualified. The SEC complaint contains allegations, and the DOJ explicitly states that an indictment is not proof of guilt and that defendants are presumed innocent unless convicted. However, the evidence is unusually consistent across the DOJ case summary, SEC complaint, and independent Guardian investigation. The sources converge on the same operational pattern: high fixed returns, recruitment commissions, purported mining revenues that allegedly did not exist, withdrawal restrictions, successive rebrands, and credibility-building through public promoters and a questionable executive persona.

## Sources and evidentiary hierarchy

The principal sources are summarized below.

| Source ID | Source | Evidentiary character | Main contribution |
|---|---|---|---|
| **S1** | U.S. Department of Justice, “HyperFund and Associated Cases” | Official government case page; includes charges, procedural updates, and legal caution | Criminal allegations, defendants, scheme period, promised returns, withdrawal blocking, case status |
| **S2** | U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, *SEC v. Lee and Chunga*, Complaint | Civil pleading; allegations rather than adjudicated findings | Detailed mechanics, financial flows, alleged misrepresentations, rebranding, CEO persona |
| **S3** | Sarah Martin, *The Guardian* | Independent investigative reporting | Verification attempts concerning “Steven Reece Lewis,” celebrity promotion, investor experience, and public context |
| **S4** | Dan Mangan, CNBC | Reputable contemporaneous news report | Summary of DOJ and SEC actions, charge descriptions, and headline loss estimates |

The SEC complaint and DOJ case page are the most important sources for the alleged mechanics because they are primary legal records or official government materials. The Guardian is particularly valuable for the independent examination of the purported CEO. CNBC provides a concise contemporaneous synthesis but adds less underlying detail than the legal filings.

## Network identity and evolution

### HyperFund’s names and rebrands

According to the DOJ, the operation was known as HyperFund, HyperTech, HyperCapital, HyperVerse, and HyperNation. The SEC describes HyperFund as launched in June 2020 by the HyperTech Group, followed by a rebranding to HyperVerse in approximately December 2021 and to HyperNation in approximately May 2022. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases); [S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

The name changes were not merely cosmetic in the promotional narrative. HyperFund was initially presented as a decentralized-finance ecosystem. HyperVerse shifted the emphasis toward a metaverse and virtual world. HyperNation subsequently adopted a political and social narrative involving a purported decentralized government, inequality, and a universal basic income. The SEC alleges that these changing themes capitalized on contemporary technology and cultural buzzwords while retaining the underlying membership and reward structure. ([S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

The available evidence therefore suggests a network that preserved continuity beneath changing branding. The SEC alleges that the back-office transition from HyperFund to HyperVerse was largely automatic for existing investors, even though users were moved to a new website and later encouraged to migrate again to HyperNation. ([S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

### Key individuals and roles

The DOJ identified three principal defendants in its criminal cases:

- **Xue Samuel Lee**, also known as Sam Lee, an Australian national residing in Dubai, whom prosecutors allege co-founded HyperFund.
- **Rodney Burton**, also known as “Bitcoin Rodney,” a Miami-based promoter.
- **Brenda Indah Chunga**, also known as “Bitcoin Beautee,” a Maryland-based promoter. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases); [S4](https://www.cnbc.com/2024/01/29/doj-and-sec-unveil-charges-in-1point9-billion-cryptocurrency-fraud-scheme.html))

The SEC separately sued Lee and Chunga in civil proceedings, alleging unregistered securities offerings and violations of the antifraud provisions of federal securities law. ([S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

Chunga’s alleged role illustrates how the network used public-facing promoters. The SEC alleges that she became a top promoter within approximately six months, reaching the “VIP 5 STAR” level, which reportedly required at least $5 million in referred investment “sales.” The complaint alleges that she received approximately $3.7 million, including about $2.5 million withdrawn from the platform and approximately $1.1 million obtained directly from investors. ([S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

## Alleged Ponzi mechanics

### High and implausible passive returns

The central investment proposition was a “membership” purchased with cryptocurrency, particularly Tether, with the membership represented internally as HyperUnits. The SEC alleges that membership levels included approximately $300, $500, $1,000, and $10,000. Investors were promised passive daily returns of 0.5% to 1%, potentially reaching two or three times their initial investment. The DOJ similarly describes promised daily returns of 0.5% to 1% until the initial investment was doubled or tripled. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases); [S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

The SEC complaint records Chunga telling prospective investors that they could recover their original investment in roughly seven months and then treat subsequent rewards as “pure profit.” This language framed the investment as passive, automatic, and largely independent of the investor’s work. ([S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

Such promised returns were not presented merely as speculative appreciation in a volatile token. They were described as regular rewards generated by the platform. The SEC alleges that the platform lacked a legitimate source of revenue sufficient to meet these obligations and that earlier investors’ withdrawals were funded by newer investor deposits. That is the defining alleged Ponzi mechanism in the case. ([S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

### Recruitment-based rewards

The system also allegedly used pyramid-style incentives. Investors could receive “accelerated” or leveraged rewards by recruiting new members. The SEC describes three reward categories: Community Rewards, VIP Rewards, and Global Rewards. Community Rewards allegedly paid commissions based on the membership value of a recruit’s downline, potentially extending through 20 levels. VIP Rewards increased returns when promoters generated specified volumes of new membership sales. Global Rewards allegedly pooled 4% of company sales for distribution to top promoters. ([S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

This structure combined two reinforcing mechanisms:

1. **Passive-return messaging**, which attracted people who were promised income without active labor; and  
2. **Recruitment compensation**, which encouraged members to bring in additional capital and expand the network.

The evidence indicates that the recruitment component was not incidental. It was a core means of generating new deposits and sustaining promotional momentum. Chunga allegedly used online seminars, Zoom presentations, videos, and personal displays of wealth to recruit investors. The SEC alleges that her promotional strategy included emphasizing her supposed earnings and luxury lifestyle. ([S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

### Claimed mining revenues

To make the returns appear economically plausible, promotional materials allegedly claimed that rewards were funded by large-scale crypto-mining operations. The DOJ states that investors were told returns would be paid from mining operations that did not exist. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases))

The SEC complaint provides a more detailed allegation: Chunga allegedly told investors that HyperTech had warehouses around the world mining Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies and generating millions of dollars. Yet the SEC alleges that Lee later admitted in a recorded 2023 call that the group had exited Bitcoin mining in 2019, before HyperFund’s launch, because mining was not profitable. The SEC further alleges that Lee acknowledged that promotional narratives about the group’s mining history were inaccurate. ([S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

If proven, this would be a particularly significant misrepresentation because the mining claim supplied the apparent external revenue source necessary to distinguish the operation from a deposit-funded scheme. The alleged absence of meaningful mining activity supports the SEC’s characterization of HyperFund as both a Ponzi and a pyramid scheme.

## Public promoters and credibility construction

The alleged scheme used promoters as a distribution and trust mechanism. The SEC describes Chunga as one of the leading U.S. promoters and alleges that recruitment materials presented Lee’s business history, media appearances, and association with blockchain companies as evidence of legitimacy. ([S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

The complaint also alleges that promotional materials falsely or misleadingly referenced relationships with DigitalX and IBM. DigitalX reportedly issued a February 2021 notice denying affiliation with HyperTech Group and its associated products, including HyperFund. The SEC separately alleges that IBM was not involved with Hcash despite promotional claims. ([S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

The use of credibility claims served a clear recruitment purpose. Chunga allegedly told prospective investors that the founders had too much public visibility and reputational exposure to disappear with investors’ money. This transformed public recognition into an implied safeguard, even though public visibility does not establish financial solvency or the existence of underlying revenue.

The Guardian independently reported that HyperVerse also used celebrity video endorsements from Steve Wozniak, Chuck Norris, Jim Norton, and Lance Bass. The Guardian found no indication that these individuals understood the investment model or knew of the alleged fraud; the messages did not themselves discuss investments or money. The article reported that the celebrities were available through Cameo, suggesting that at least some endorsements may have been paid promotional appearances rather than independent due diligence. ([S3](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist))

## The questionable CEO persona

### “Steven Reece Lewis”

HyperVerse’s December 2021 launch introduced a purported CEO named “Steven Reece Lewis.” Promotional materials reportedly claimed that he had attended the University of Leeds and the University of Cambridge, worked at Goldman Sachs, sold a web-development company to Adobe, and founded an IT start-up. ([S3](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist))

The Guardian reported that it could not verify these claims. It stated that the universities had no record of him under that name, Companies House and SEC records contained no matching record, Adobe filings did not show the alleged acquisition, and Goldman Sachs reportedly found no record of his employment. ([S3](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist))

The SEC complaint goes further, alleging that “Steven Reece Lewis” was not a genuine CEO but a paid actor portraying a fabricated character. According to the complaint, the actor worked as a television presenter who helped businesses front their products and services. The SEC alleges that Lee knew or recklessly disregarded that the supposed CEO was not an actual executive. ([S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

This alleged persona was strategically useful. It gave HyperVerse a new leadership figure at the precise moment of rebranding, creating the impression of institutional continuity and professional management. It also helped shift public attention from the earlier HyperFund model toward a technologically ambitious metaverse project.

## Withdrawal problems and collapse

The evidence indicates a progressive deterioration in investor access to funds. The DOJ states that HyperFund began blocking withdrawals in at least July 2021. The SEC complaint provides a somewhat different timeline, alleging that investors experienced withdrawal difficulties in November or December 2021, were generally unable to withdraw by February or March 2022, and ultimately could not redeem investments after November 2022 when the HOO Exchange stopped functioning. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases); [S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

The withdrawal process itself was allegedly complicated. Investors had to convert HyperUnits into Molecular Future tokens, transfer those tokens to the HOO Exchange, convert them again, and then seek fiat currency. The SEC alleges that HyperUnits appeared to be valued at $1 when deposited but were not similarly pegged when converted for withdrawal. It further states that Molecular Future was quoted at approximately $0.00001949 on September 4, 2023, illustrating the alleged disconnect between the platform’s internal valuation and realizable market value. ([S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

The pattern is consistent with an operation that could display account balances without possessing equivalent liquid assets. Rebranding and technical explanations for withdrawal delays may have delayed recognition of the collapse and encouraged investors to remain engaged.

## Scale and legal status

The reported scale varies by source. CNBC describes the DOJ case as involving approximately $1.9 billion, while the DOJ case page refers to approximately $1.89 billion. The SEC complaint alleges that more than $1.7 billion was raised worldwide. These figures should not be treated as identical measurements; they may reflect different calculation methods, periods, or evidentiary thresholds. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases); [S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11); [S4](https://www.cnbc.com/2024/01/29/doj-and-sec-unveil-charges-in-1point9-billion-cryptocurrency-fraud-scheme.html))

As of the DOJ page supplied, Chunga pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit securities and wire fraud. Burton was sentenced on July 23, 2026, to 32 months’ imprisonment, followed by three years of supervised release. The same page states that Lee was charged with conspiracy to commit securities and wire fraud, while Chunga also faced SEC civil claims. The DOJ page lists Chunga’s sentencing as continued to January 7, 2027. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases))

The legal posture matters: Chunga’s guilty plea and Burton’s sentence are procedurally different from the SEC’s allegations against Lee and Chunga. The report should therefore distinguish established procedural events from allegations about the scheme’s operation.

## Contradictions and unresolved issues

### Amount raised

The principal numerical discrepancy is the amount allegedly raised: $1.7 billion in the SEC complaint, $1.89 billion on the DOJ case page, and approximately $1.9 billion in CNBC’s headline and summary. The sources agree on extraordinary scale but do not establish one definitive figure. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases); [S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11); [S4](https://www.cnbc.com/2024/01/29/doj-and-sec-unveil-charges-in-1point9-billion-cryptocurrency-fraud-scheme.html))

### Withdrawal timeline

The DOJ identifies July 2021 as the beginning of blocked withdrawals, whereas the SEC describes serious withdrawal problems beginning in late 2021, with broader inability to withdraw by February or March 2022. These accounts may refer to different forms or stages of restriction, but the supplied sources do not resolve the difference. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases); [S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

### Identity of the actor

The SEC alleges that the actor behind “Steven Reece Lewis” lived in Bangkok and worked as a television presenter. The Guardian independently reported that the persona could not be verified, but its account does not establish the actor’s legal identity. The stronger claim—that the persona was fabricated and performed by a paid actor—comes from the SEC complaint and remains an allegation unless adjudicated. ([S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11); [S3](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist))

## Conclusion

The most persuasive interpretation of the available evidence is that HyperFund/HyperVerse operated as a recruitment-driven investment network whose apparent legitimacy depended on coordinated storytelling. The promised returns supplied the economic attraction; the referral system supplied new participants and deposits; alleged mining operations supplied a purported external revenue explanation; public promoters supplied interpersonal trust; rebranding supplied continuity after operational problems; and the questionable CEO persona supplied an image of professional leadership.

The sources do not justify treating every promotional celebrity or participant as knowingly complicit. Nor do they eliminate legal uncertainty regarding individual culpability. Nevertheless, taken together, the evidence strongly supports the assessment that the network’s central architecture was not a functioning crypto-mining investment business but an alleged Ponzi-pyramid model sustained by recruitment, claims of nonexistent or inadequate revenue, and repeated efforts to preserve investor confidence after withdrawals became restricted.
